title: The Photograph
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: The albums arrived on a Wednesday afternoon. Three volumes, dark green cloth, bound over eighty years by an aunt Astrid had barely known. She opened the first at random — a family photograph from 1943. Four people. The caption named all four. In the doorway of the house behind them, in shadow, in a dark dress, looking directly at the camera, was a fifth.

chapters.title: Aunt Vera
chapters.body:
The albums arrived on a Wednesday afternoon.

Astrid Lindqvist was forty-one, and she had, that spring, been asked by her mother to sort through the contents of Aunt Vera's flat in Stockholm. Aunt Vera had died in February at eighty-three, in her small apartment on Karlbergsvägen, of nothing in particular — old age, the doctor had said, in the specific gentle way Swedish doctors used the phrase when they meant that a woman who had been declining for years had, at last, quietly stopped — and had left, in her will, the majority of her small estate to Astrid's mother, who was Vera's younger sister, along with the specific instruction that her personal papers and photographs were to be given to Astrid.

Astrid was Vera's only niece. Astrid's mother had, throughout Astrid's life, spoken of Vera in the small careful way one spoke of a much older sister who had never married and who had lived a small independent life at some professional distance — Vera had been, throughout Astrid's childhood, an infrequent presence at holidays, a small polite Christmas card, and a specific green wool cardigan she had knitted for Astrid at seven and had, thereafter, never mentioned. Astrid had not, so far as she could remember, ever had a long conversation with her aunt.

She had, on receiving the will, been surprised that Vera had thought of her at all.

She had, on the Wednesday afternoon in April, come home to her flat in Södermalm to find the two large cardboard boxes on the small landing outside her door. The movers who had cleared out Vera's apartment had, according to her mother, arranged for the boxes to be delivered. They contained, according to her mother, whatever photographs and papers Vera had kept — the boxes were the sum total, more or less, of what a woman leaves after eighty-three years of a small orderly life.

Astrid had brought the boxes inside.

She had, that evening, opened the first one.

It had contained, mostly, small brown envelopes of family photographs, arranged in no particular order but tied together in small bundles with string. It had contained a small stack of Vera's employment records from the university library where Vera had worked for forty years. It had contained a small collection of postcards, tied together with a green ribbon, from various places Vera had visited on her holidays in the sixties and seventies. It had contained, at the bottom, three photograph albums.

The albums had been bound in dark green cloth. They had had, on their spines, in small gold lettering that had faded over the years, the words *Familj* followed by three ranges of dates. *Familj 1936–1955.* *Familj 1956–1980.* *Familj 1981–2020.*

Astrid had, that evening, opened the first album.

—

The first album had been, as she had expected, a small conventional family album of the mid-twentieth century.

It had begun with a small brown photograph of Vera and Astrid's mother as small girls — Vera perhaps eight, Astrid's mother perhaps three — standing together in the small garden of their childhood house outside Uppsala. The photograph had been dated, in Vera's small careful hand in white ink in the margin, *sommaren 1936.* Astrid had smiled at it. She had seen the photograph before, in a small copy that her mother had kept on the mantel.

She had turned the page.

The following pages had shown the small usual progression of Vera's childhood and adolescence — school portraits, holidays at a small lake house Astrid's family had never spoken of, small birthday gatherings, small Christmases. The photographs had been arranged in a small careful chronological order, each with its small careful caption in white ink beneath it.

Astrid had, for perhaps forty minutes, turned the pages of the first album with the small quiet pleasure of a woman looking at photographs of her family from before her own time. She had noted, from time to time, small details that pleased her — her grandmother's specific dress in a photograph from 1938, her mother's specific small stubborn expression at four in a photograph from 1939. She had, occasionally, said aloud to herself, in the small quiet flat: *there you are, mother.*

She had reached a photograph from the autumn of 1943.

The photograph had shown the small family — Astrid's grandmother, her grandfather, Vera at fifteen, her mother at ten — standing in front of the small house in Uppsala on what had been, according to the caption, the first day of school. The four of them had been standing in a small careful arrangement, in the small careful way of a Swedish family being photographed by a neighbor with a small folding camera. They had been smiling. Vera had been holding her small leather satchel. Astrid's mother had been holding a small doll.

Behind them, in the doorway of the house, had been a fifth person.

Astrid had not, on first looking at the photograph, noticed the fifth person. She had, on second looking, noticed her.

The fifth person had been a woman. She had been standing in the specific small doorway of the house, in the shadow, so that she had not been immediately visible against the interior. She had been wearing, so far as Astrid could tell, a dark dress. She had been holding, so far as Astrid could tell, one hand at her waist and one hand at her side. She had been looking directly at the camera.

She had not been smiling.

Astrid had, for perhaps a full minute, looked at the small dark figure in the doorway.

She had thought: *a housekeeper. My grandparents must have had a housekeeper.*

She had thought: *or a friend of my grandmother's. Or a neighbor who was, at that moment, visiting. Or an aunt of my grandfather's.*

She had thought, at last: *someone in the family whom no one mentioned.*

The specific stillness of the small dark figure in the doorway — the specific small definite fact that she had, in a photograph clearly composed for the family in front, been standing in the doorway of the house and had been included in the frame — had, over the course of Astrid's minute of looking, become slowly more specific.

She had, at last, looked at the caption beneath the photograph.

The caption, in Vera's small careful hand in white ink, had read:

*Första skoldagen, 1943. Mor, Far, jag, Karin.*

*First day of school, 1943. Mother, Father, me, Karin.*

Karin had been the name of Astrid's mother.

There had been no fifth name in the caption.

Astrid had, sitting on her sofa in her flat in Södermalm on a Wednesday evening in April, looked at the caption for a long moment.

She had, then, looked at the photograph.

She had, then, looked at the caption again.

The fifth person in the doorway had been, unmistakably, in the frame of the photograph. The caption had, unmistakably, named only four people.

Astrid had gotten up.

She had walked into her small kitchen. She had made herself a cup of tea. She had come back to the sitting room. She had sat down.

She had opened the album again.

She had turned to the photograph.

The fifth person had been in the doorway. In the same dark dress. In the same small still posture. Looking, from the shadow of the interior, directly at the camera.

Astrid had, in the small quiet of her sitting room, told herself several plausible things.

She had told herself that the fifth person was a servant, or a neighbor, or an aunt, and that Vera had, in captioning the photograph for her own personal album, listed only the immediate family because that was, from Vera's perspective, who the photograph was of. She had told herself that this was a small ordinary omission in a small ordinary album.

She had told herself, further, that she was tired.

She had told herself that she should close the album, and finish her tea, and go to bed, and look at the album again tomorrow.

She had turned the page.

—

The next photograph had been from Christmas 1943.

It had shown the small family gathered around a small dining table. Vera at fifteen, Astrid's mother at ten, Astrid's grandparents at the ends of the table. A small Christmas ham in the middle. Small candles. Small Swedish decorations.

Behind the table, in the small doorway to the kitchen, had been the fifth person. In the same dark dress.

Astrid had turned the page.

Easter 1944. The family in the garden. In the small doorway to the house — the fifth person.

Astrid had turned the page.

Summer 1944. A family holiday at the lake house. Vera and Astrid's mother in swimming costumes on a small dock. In the far background, on the porch of the small lake house, standing in the shadow of the eaves — the fifth person.

Astrid had turned the pages, faster.

Christmas 1944. Winter 1945. Easter 1945.

The fifth person was in every photograph.

She was, in every photograph, in a doorway or on a porch or on the far side of a room, in shadow, in a dark dress, looking directly at the camera. She was, in every photograph, so slightly present that a casual viewer would not, at a first glance, have noticed her. She was, in every photograph, precisely visible enough to have been noticed, once one had noticed her once.

Astrid had turned back to the first photograph, from 1936. The very first photograph of Vera and Astrid's mother in the garden.

She had, on this second looking, seen the small dark figure in the doorway of the house at the far edge of the frame.

The fifth person had, so far as Astrid could tell, been in every photograph in the album, from 1936 onward.

—

She had put the album down.

She had, in the small quiet of her sitting room, gotten up and walked to the window and looked out at the street. The street had been ordinary. A small tired man had been walking a small tired dog. The lights had been coming on in the flats across the way.

She had thought, in the specific small quiet way of a woman not permitting herself to think anything too quickly: *I need to look at the other albums.*

She had gone back to the sofa.

She had, from the second box, taken out the second album — *Familj 1956–1980* — and had opened it.

The second album had begun with a photograph from 1956 that had shown Vera at twenty-eight, at her graduation from the library sciences program at Uppsala University. She had been standing in the small square in front of the university with a small group of her classmates. She had been smiling.

Behind her, at the far edge of the frame, standing on the steps of a small building across the square in the shadow of the doorway — the fifth person.

Astrid had turned the pages.

Vera at thirty. Vera at thirty-five. Vera at forty. Vera on a small holiday in Copenhagen in 1963. Vera on a small holiday in Berlin in 1967. Vera on a small holiday in Rome in 1972. Vera at Astrid's parents' wedding in 1979 — a photograph in which the young Astrid's mother was in her white dress, holding Astrid's father's hand, standing on the steps of a small church in Stockholm.

In every photograph of Vera the fifth person was present.

In the photograph of Astrid's parents' wedding, the fifth person had been standing on the far side of the church steps, in the small dark doorway of a side entrance, in the same dark dress. Looking at the camera.

Astrid had, at this photograph, done what she had, until then, not permitted herself to do.

She had, in the specific small careful way, looked at the fifth person's face.

The face had been small in the photograph. It had been half in shadow. It had, all the same, been resolvable.

The face had been a woman of perhaps forty. It had had dark hair, drawn back. It had had, so far as Astrid could tell, a small still expression that was not, exactly, sad, but was also not, in any small way, at peace. It had been, in some quality Astrid could not have named, familiar.

Astrid had looked at the face for a long moment.

She had, at last, understood why it was familiar.

She had looked at her own reflection in the small dark screen of the television across the room, and had, in the specific small careful way one did such comparisons, compared her own face to the face of the woman in the doorway.

They had, allowing for the small differences of period and hair, been the same face.

—

Astrid had, that night, not slept much.

She had, at three in the morning, gotten up from her bed and had gone into the sitting room and had opened the third album — *Familj 1981–2020.*

She had gone through it, page by page, at three in the morning, in the small yellow light of the reading lamp beside the sofa.

The third album had begun with a photograph from 1981 — a photograph, Astrid had realized after a moment, of her own christening. Vera had been present. Astrid at three months had been in her mother's arms. Vera had been on the far side of her mother, looking at the small child with a specific small careful attention Astrid had not, until that moment, known Vera had ever paid her.

Behind them, in the doorway to the vestibule of the church — the fifth person. In the same dark dress. Looking at the camera.

Astrid had turned the pages.

Her third birthday. Her fifth. Her seventh. Vera at the small parties, on the small edges, taking, apparently, the small photographs that she was, in this album, sometimes also in. Astrid had, from the photographs of Vera at the parties, understood that Vera had been more present in Astrid's early childhood than she had, herself, remembered — that Vera had, throughout Astrid's first ten years, come to the family gatherings, taken photographs, been at the edges of the small family life.

She had also, at some point in the mid-nineties, stopped.

The photographs of Vera had, after 1994, become less frequent, and had, by 2000, ceased. The album had continued — Astrid at fourteen, at seventeen, at twenty-one, at graduation, in her small first apartment — but Vera had not been in any of the photographs from that point on. The photographs had, presumably, been taken by Astrid's parents, or by Astrid herself, and had been sent to Vera, who had kept them in the album at some ongoing distance.

The fifth person had been in every photograph.

Every photograph. Through Astrid's whole childhood and adolescence and young adulthood. In doorways of houses she had lived in, on porches of houses she had visited, on the edges of school events, on the small edges of family gatherings. The fifth person had been in the background of the photographs from her wedding — Astrid had, at twenty-nine, married a man she had, at thirty-two, divorced — and the fifth person had been on the edge of every photograph of Astrid's small marriage.

The fifth person had been, over the fifty-four years of the three albums, aging.

Very slowly. Almost imperceptibly, from photograph to photograph. But Astrid, at three in the morning, going carefully through the three albums in order, had been able to see it. The fifth person in 1936 had been perhaps thirty. The fifth person in 1943 had been perhaps thirty-two. The fifth person in 1979, at Astrid's parents' wedding, had been perhaps forty. The fifth person in 2000, in the last photograph in which Vera herself had appeared, had been perhaps forty-eight.

The fifth person in the last photograph in the album — a photograph from 2019, of Astrid at forty, at a small party for her mother's seventy-fifth birthday — had been perhaps fifty-five.

The fifth person had, over eighty years of Astrid's family history, aged about twenty-five years.

Astrid had, at three-thirty in the morning of the Thursday, closed the third album.

She had, in the small quiet of her flat, said aloud: *what.*

She had, then, said, more quietly: *who are you.*

The album had not answered.

The albums had, at last, been what they had always been — a small careful record of a small orderly Swedish family, kept over eight decades by a small careful librarian who had never married, and who had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who kept records, recorded everything she had seen, including — apparently — the fifth person who had been standing in every doorway of every house of every event of every year of that family's life.

Astrid had, at last, gone back to bed.

She had, at four in the morning, thought, before she slept: *Vera saw her too.*

She had, at four-fifteen, thought: *Vera saw her, and she photographed her, and she kept the photographs, and she left them to me.*

She had, at four-thirty, understood the shape of what Vera had done.

Vera had, at some point in her long careful life, understood that she was being followed. She had, at some point, decided to keep a record of it. She had, throughout the eighty years of her life, taken photographs — of the family, of herself, of the small ordinary events — and had, in every photograph, included the follower. She had made a small careful eighty-year archive of a woman who had been standing in the family's doorways since 1936.

And Vera had, at her death, left the archive to Astrid.

Vera had, in the specific small careful way she had understood something to be true, believed that Astrid was going to need it.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.body:
The letter had been in the third album.

Astrid had, on the Thursday morning, gone through the third album a second time, in the specific careful way she had gone through the first two the previous night. She had, this time, been looking not only at the fifth person but at everything else — for any small note, any small margin comment, any small indication from Vera about what she had known.

She had, between two of the last pages of the album, found the small folded piece of paper.

It had been a letter. It had been written, in Vera's small careful hand, on a small piece of the same specific pale blue notepaper Vera had used for her small polite Christmas cards throughout Astrid's childhood. It had been folded, in the small precise way of a woman who folded things carefully, into thirds. It had been addressed, on the outside, in Vera's hand:

*To Astrid.*

Astrid had, that morning, at her kitchen table with a cup of coffee, opened the letter.

—

*My dear Astrid,*

*If you are reading this, it is because you have gone through the albums and have seen her.*

*I have wondered, over the last many years, whether you would see her. I have wondered whether the family had, in you, produced another one of us — another one of the small careful sort of person who notices when something is present in a photograph that ought not to be. I did not, for a long time, know whether you were such a person. Your mother is not. Your father was not. Your grandmother, my mother, was not.*

*But I was. And, I have come to understand, my aunt Karin was.*

*I do not know if you knew that our mother had an older sister. Karin was born in 1910, ten years before our mother. She was, in the family stories, a difficult woman. She never married. She lived in Uppsala for the whole of her life. She died in 1955, of what was, at the time, called nervous exhaustion, and was, more likely, what we would now call depression combined with — with, I think, what she saw. She died when I was twenty-seven. I had, in the last years of her life, spent some time with her. She had, in those years, tried to prepare me for what she had already understood was going to happen to me.*

*It had happened to her. She had, from her childhood onward, been aware of a woman who was, at all times, at the edges of her life. Standing in doorways. Sitting at the far end of long tables. On the far side of trains. She had not, ever, spoken to Karin. She had not, ever, made any small demand. She had only been present, at the small edges of every photograph of every event of Karin's entire life, and had, over the course of that life, slowly aged.*

*Karin had, in her forties, begun to photograph her. She had done this in the small careful way of a librarian's daughter — she had kept an album. She had taken the album with her when she went to Uppsala. She had, in her last visit before she died, given it to me. She had said, at the door of her small apartment: 'you will need this someday.' She had, I have come to understand, been right.*

*I have, since 1955, been the one at the edges of the family who has, in my own life, been followed.*

*The one who followed Karin followed me from the day of Karin's funeral. I do not know if she was, in some way, the same one. She may have been. Karin's follower was, when Karin died, a woman of perhaps sixty. My follower, when she appeared to me in 1955, was a woman of perhaps thirty. I have thought, over the years, that this may be a specific characteristic of the — of the followers, that they begin again at a certain age when the person they have been following dies. I do not know whether this is right. I only know that the woman who has been in my photographs was not, when she began, the same age as the woman who had been in Karin's.*

*I have, over the sixty-five years since 1955, learned certain things about her.*

*She has never spoken to me. She has never approached me. She has never made any small indication that she wants any specific thing from me. She has, however, in some small careful way, expected me to be aware of her. I have, over the years, come to understand this from the way she stands. She stands, in the doorways of every place I have lived and every place I have visited, in the specific patient way of a person who has been waiting for someone to notice her, and who has, at some point in her long patience, ceased to expect that anyone will.*

*I have noticed her. I have, throughout my life, noticed her. But I have not, at any point, spoken to her.*

*I do not know if I regret this.*

*I have, in the last decade of my life, come to believe that she is not, in the way I first feared, a threat. She has not, in eighty years, harmed anyone. She has not, in eighty years, done anything at all. She has, so far as I can tell, only been present. She has stood at the small edges of my life for as long as I have been alive, and she has, in her own small way, watched.*

*I have come to think that this is her only occupation. That she is, in some sense, a — an observer. That she has been assigned to the family, or to me, or to whoever in the family can see her, and that her task is to see.*

*I do not know who assigned her. I do not know why she was assigned. I do not know whether there is, in some ledger somewhere, a small careful record being made of everything she has, over eighty years, seen. I suspect there is. But I do not know.*

*I write to you now because I have understood, over the last several years, that when I die, she will pass to you.*

*I have understood this from a small change in her behavior over the last decade. She has, since perhaps 2010, been standing not only in the doorways of my life, but at the small edges of yours. She has been in the photographs I have taken of you, and in the photographs I have received of you from your mother. She has been at your wedding. She has been at the parties for your mother's birthday. She has been at your small first apartment.*

*She has, in short, been preparing.*

*She is going to, at some point after my death, appear to you. She will not, at first, be visible in the small ordinary way. She will be visible only in photographs. You will notice her, first, in a photograph — perhaps in one of the albums I have left you, perhaps in a photograph of your own — and you will, upon noticing her, begin to notice her in others. And she will, over the following months and years, come slowly closer.*

*By the time she is in your ordinary field of vision, you will have been aware of her for perhaps a year. This is, I have come to understand, how it works. She does not, in the courtesy of her position, come suddenly. She comes gradually, so as to permit you to become used to her.*

*I have left you the albums so that you can see her early. I have left you this letter so that you will understand what you are seeing.*

*I want, in this letter, to say two more things.*

*The first is that you are permitted, if you wish, to try to speak to her. I did not. I chose not to, throughout my life, because I was Karin's niece and Karin had, in her last years, warned me against it. Karin had believed that to speak to the follower was to acknowledge a debt to her, and that acknowledging the debt would produce further demands. I do not, at the end of my life, know whether Karin was right. It is possible that the follower would, if spoken to, respond kindly. It is possible she would not. I have not tested it. I mention this only because you are not obliged to make the same choice I made.*

*The second is that you are permitted, if you wish, to try to pass her on.*

*This too Karin told me. Karin had, in her last months, come to believe that the follower could, under certain circumstances, be transferred to another person who could see her. She had not, in her own case, done this — she had not, she said, had a niece to pass her to. I have not, in mine, either. You are the person to whom she has been passed. If, at some point in your future, you become aware of a young girl in the family who is another one of us — another small careful person who notices what should not be noticed — you may, in the specific way that Karin left the first album to me and I have left the three albums to you, prepare her. You may pass the follower on.*

*You are not obliged to. You may, if you wish, be the last of us. She will, in that case, be with you for the rest of your life. She will, upon your death, presumably choose a new person from another family entirely, or she will, perhaps, cease to follow anyone. I do not know. But if you wish for the family to be, at last, done with her, you may simply not prepare anyone. She will, in that case, end with you.*

*I have not decided which of these is better. I have not, in eighty-three years, been able to decide.*

*I leave the decision to you.*

*I have loved you, my Astrid. I have not, in your life, been able to show this as often as I would have liked. I have, in the small careful way of a woman with a small careful life, kept my distance. I have kept my distance in part because I did not want to burden you with the small careful weight of what I knew before you needed to know it. I have, in another part, kept my distance because I have not, throughout my life, learned very well how to love the people I have loved.*

*I regret this. I have, in the last years of my life, understood that the small careful distance I kept from you was not, as I told myself, a way of protecting you. It was a way of protecting me. I have been sorry for this. I have wanted to write it to you.*

*You will understand what to do.*

*Your aunt,*

*Vera.*

—

Astrid had, at her kitchen table on Thursday morning, put the letter down.

She had, for a long moment, done nothing.

She had, at last, gotten up. She had washed her face at the sink. She had come back to the kitchen. She had drunk a glass of water. She had picked up the letter and had read it a second time.

She had, on the second reading, sat with it.

She had thought about Aunt Karin, whom she had not known had existed. She had thought about the woman in the photograph of the first day of school in 1943, in the doorway of her grandparents' house, looking at the camera. She had thought about Vera at twenty-seven, sitting in Karin's small apartment in Uppsala in the last months of Karin's life, receiving from her aunt a small album and a small warning and, presumably, a small letter of her own, which Vera had, at that moment in 1955, presumably not entirely believed.

She had thought about the fact that she had, since receiving the albums the previous afternoon, spent a total of perhaps nine hours with them.

She had thought about the fact that, according to Vera, this was the beginning of what would be, from now on, the whole of her life.

She had gotten up. She had gone into her sitting room. She had, without particular reason, walked to the window and had looked out.

The street had been ordinary. The small tired man had been walking his small tired dog again — perhaps a routine of his, at this hour of the morning — and the lights in the windows across the way had been coming on in the small careful way of a Stockholm morning in April.

Astrid had, standing at her window, looked at the small doorway of the building across the street.

The doorway had been empty.

She had looked at the small doorway of the building next to it.

The doorway had been empty.

She had, all the same, stood at her window for perhaps ten minutes, looking at every doorway on the small street, until she had understood that she had, without meaning to, been looking for the follower.

She had, at last, drawn the curtains.

She had gone to work.

chapters.title: Doorways
chapters.body:
She saw her the first time in a photograph.

It was on a Sunday in June, three months after receiving the albums. She had, over those three months, gone through the albums many times. She had, over those three months, taken very few photographs of her own — she had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had received a warning, been reluctant to introduce new images into the situation. She had, when she had taken photographs, taken them of small ordinary things: her lunch on a Saturday, a small view of the water at Slussen from a bench she liked, a small selfie she had sent to her mother from a birthday dinner.

None of the photographs had shown the follower.

Astrid had, over the three months, begun to hope that Vera had been mistaken. That the follower was a phenomenon that had been specific to Vera and to Karin, and that Astrid, though she had inherited the album, had not inherited the woman. She had, over the three months, begun to relax.

On the Sunday in June, at a small brunch with her mother in a small café on Södermalm, her mother had asked her to take a photograph of the two of them.

Astrid had done it. She had held her phone at arm's length, and had, in the small careful way one took such photographs, framed her mother and herself against the small window of the café behind them. She had taken the photograph. She had shown it to her mother. Her mother had, in her small pleasant way, approved of it.

Astrid had, later that afternoon, in her flat, been going through the photographs on her phone in the small ordinary way one does. She had reached the photograph from the café.

She had, on this second looking, seen the woman in the doorway behind them.

The doorway had been the small door of the café's kitchen, at the far end of the small dining room, behind her mother's shoulder. The door had been slightly open. In the small dark gap of the door had been a woman. She had been standing in the shadow. She had been wearing the same dark dress. She had been looking at the camera.

Astrid had, sitting on her sofa in her flat on a Sunday afternoon in June, felt, for the first time since she had read Vera's letter, the small definite chill of the specific thing being confirmed.

She had gone into the kitchen. She had, at her small kitchen table, opened the third album to the last page. She had looked at the woman in the last photograph — Astrid at forty, at the party for her mother's seventy-fifth birthday, in 2019.

She had compared the two women.

The woman in the doorway of the café in June was, so far as she could tell, perhaps six years older than the woman in the party photograph from 2019. She had aged, in three years, six years. She was, in the language of the phenomenon Vera had described, arriving.

—

She had, over the following six months, seen the woman in perhaps forty photographs.

She had begun, in the fourth month, to take photographs deliberately — to test the phenomenon, to see whether it was consistent, to see whether it would appear in every photograph she took or only in some. She had taken small photographs of her flat, of the courtyard behind the building, of her walk to work, of the small park where she sometimes ate her lunch.

The woman had appeared in perhaps three-quarters of them.

She had appeared, always, in a doorway or on an edge — the entrance to a shop, the far end of a corridor, the small dark gap between two buildings across a courtyard. She had always been in the same dark dress. She had always been looking at the camera. She had, over the six months, continued to age slightly — she had, by December, been perhaps sixty-five, whereas at the party photograph in 2019 she had been perhaps fifty-five.

Astrid had, over those six months, developed a small careful vocabulary for thinking about her.

She had, in her private thinking, come to call the woman *the observer*. Not, as Karin and Vera had, *the follower* — Astrid had, over her small careful analysis of the photographs, come to understand that the woman was not following her in any active sense. The woman was, rather, present. She was already, when Astrid arrived somewhere, in the doorway. She was already, when Astrid left, still in the doorway. She did not move. She did not, so far as Astrid could determine, transit from doorway to doorway in any way an ordinary person would. She was simply, at every place Astrid took a photograph, already in the frame.

Astrid had, in the sixth month, taken a photograph in her mother's kitchen while visiting for a Sunday lunch.

The observer had been in the doorway to the small pantry.

Astrid had, that Sunday afternoon, quietly asked her mother whether her mother could see anything unusual in the photograph.

Her mother had looked at it.

Her mother had said: *what am I supposed to see?*

Astrid had said: *anything.*

Her mother had said: *your niece is going to have to help me with these questions. What do you mean, dear?*

Astrid had said: *nothing. Never mind.*

Her mother had put down the phone.

Astrid had understood, that afternoon, that her mother was not one of them. That her mother had been in the family for seventy-six years and had never, at any point, seen the observer in any photograph.

The observer was visible only to Karin, and to Vera, and now to Astrid.

—

She had, in the twelfth month after Vera's death, seen the observer for the first time in ordinary sight.

It had happened at the bus stop on Ringvägen on a Tuesday morning in February — one year almost to the day since Vera had died. Astrid had been waiting for the number four bus. She had, in the small habit she had developed over the last several months of watching for the observer at the edges of any place she found herself, glanced at the small doorway of the shop across the street.

The observer had been standing in the doorway.

Not in a photograph. In the small ordinary street, at eight-fifteen in the morning, in the small pale February light of Stockholm, in the shadow of the small doorway of the tobacconist across the street.

She had been looking at Astrid.

Astrid had, for a long moment, stood at the bus stop.

She had, at last, done what she had, over the year, been considering.

She had crossed the street.

She had walked, slowly, up to the doorway of the tobacconist. The observer had not moved. The observer had watched her come with the specific small still expression Astrid had, over the last year, come to know from perhaps two hundred photographs — a small still expression that was not exactly patient and was not exactly kind, but that was, so far as Astrid could interpret it, *attentive.*

Astrid had, at the doorway, stopped.

She had said, quietly, in Swedish: *hello.*

The observer had, for the first time in any of the images Astrid had ever seen of her, altered her expression very slightly. The small still attention had become, for a small moment, a small careful surprise.

She had, then, quite quietly, said, in a voice that was ordinary and small and Swedish:

*Hello, Astrid.*

Astrid had, standing on Ringvägen at eight-fifteen in the morning, felt her breath leave her.

She had, after a long moment, said: *you have never spoken.*

The observer had said: *no.*

Astrid had said: *why not.*

The observer had said, in the specific small careful voice of a woman answering a question she had been prepared for: *because I have not, in ninety years, been spoken to first.*

Astrid had said: *not by Karin.*

The observer had said: *no.*

Astrid had said: *not by Vera.*

The observer had said: *no.*

Astrid had said, more quietly: *you have been in every doorway of my family for ninety years, and you have never been spoken to.*

The observer had said, quietly: *no.*

Astrid had stood at the doorway.

She had, at last, said: *what do you want.*

The observer had said: *nothing.*

Astrid had said: *why are you here.*

The observer had said: *I have been assigned.*

Astrid had said: *by whom.*

The observer had said: *I do not know.*

Astrid had said: *what are you assigned to do.*

The observer had said: *to be present.*

Astrid had, for a very long moment, been silent.

She had, at last, said: *is that all.*

The observer had said: *yes.*

Astrid had said: *have you — have you enjoyed it.*

The observer had, at this question, been silent for a long time.

She had, at last, said: *no one has ever asked me that.*

Astrid had waited.

The observer had said, in the specific small careful voice of a woman who had, for ninety years, thought about a question she had not been asked: *I have not, exactly, enjoyed it. I have, over the years, come to know your family. I have watched Karin as a small girl. I have watched Vera. I have watched your mother, who has not been able to see me, and who has been, in my ninety years of watching, a very kind and quiet woman whom I have grown to love. I have watched you.*

She had said: *I have watched you at every birthday of your life. I have watched you at your wedding. I have watched you, over the last three years, sit alone in your flat at night and read Vera's albums and think about what you were going to say to me.*

She had said: *I have not, in that watching, been happy or unhappy. But I have not been alone.*

Astrid had said: *and if you were released.*

The observer had said: *released.*

Astrid had said: *if — Vera said you could be passed on. To another person in another generation. Or that you could be — that if I did not pass you on, you would — you would end with me. What did she mean.*

The observer had said, in the same small careful voice: *she meant that if you name a successor to me, I will move to that successor when you die. If you do not, I will remain until you die, and will then — I do not know what will happen. I have been assigned only to your family. When there is no one to see me and no one has named a successor, I will presumably be reassigned.*

Astrid had said: *and if I named — if I named you free.*

The observer had said: *pardon?*

Astrid had said: *if I said — I do not name a successor, and I release you. Now. Not at my death. Now.*

The observer had, at this, been quiet for a long moment.

She had said: *I do not know if that is possible.*

Astrid had said: *would you want it.*

The observer had said, at last: *I do not know.*

Astrid had said: *have you, in ninety years, thought about what you would do if you were released.*

The observer had said, in the small quiet voice that Astrid had come to understand was her whole voice: *no. I have not thought about it. I have not permitted myself to think about it. It would have been, throughout ninety years, a thought that would have made the watching much more difficult than it has been.*

Astrid had, at the doorway of the small tobacconist on Ringvägen, understood something.

She had understood that the observer had, throughout ninety years, been a small careful worker. She had done what she had been assigned to do. She had, in the specific small way of a person doing a small careful job for a very long time, made her peace with it, and had not, over the decades, permitted herself to want anything different. And Astrid had, in her small unpremeditated way, offered her something.

Astrid had, standing at the doorway, said: *I am not going to name a successor.*

The observer had said: *ah.*

Astrid had said: *I do not want to. I do not know anyone in the family who is like Karin, or like Vera, or like me. And even if I did, I do not want to prepare a small child now to receive you when I die. I do not want to be Vera to some future Astrid. I want, in my own way, for this to end.*

She had said: *but I do not want it to end with you.*

She had said: *I mean — I do not want it to end with you being reassigned to another family. I do not want it to end with you being alone. I want, if it is possible, for it to end with — with you being permitted, at last, to do something else.*

The observer had, at this, done something Astrid would remember for the rest of her life.

The observer had cried.

She had cried quietly, in the small careful way of a woman who had not cried in ninety years and who had, in that ninety years, forgotten how to cry loudly. She had cried in the doorway of the tobacconist while Astrid had stood in front of her on Ringvägen at eight-twenty in the morning of a Tuesday in February. She had cried, so far as Astrid could tell, out of a specific small relief that Astrid had, in her small careful way, said the specific words she had needed to hear.

She had said, at last: *thank you.*

Astrid had said: *you are welcome.*

The observer had said, more quietly: *I do not know what will happen. I do not know if I can be released. But I have — I have been offered, at last, an alternative to the watching, and I have not been offered one in ninety years, and I am — I am, at this moment, grateful to you for it.*

Astrid had said, quietly: *what do we do.*

The observer had said: *I do not know.*

Astrid had said: *we could try.*

The observer had said: *what.*

Astrid had said: *we could — we could try to release you. I could — I could, in the small formal way, say the words. I release you from your assignment to my family. I do not name a successor. I ask, in the small formal way one asks anything of a system whose rules one does not know, that you be permitted to do something else with your time.*

The observer had, at this, looked at her with a small small careful hope.

Astrid had said, quietly, on the pavement outside the small tobacconist on Ringvägen: *I release you.*

The observer had, at those words, for a very small moment, seemed to lighten. Not in any dramatic way. Not in any way that would have been visible to any passer-by. But in the specific small way of a person who had been holding a heavy small weight for ninety years and had, at that moment, been permitted to set it down.

She had said, in the small careful voice: *thank you, Astrid.*

She had, then, in the specific small ordinary way of a person turning to walk away, turned and walked away. She had walked, slowly, along Ringvägen in the direction of the water. She had, at the corner, turned. She had, from the corner, given Astrid a small careful wave. She had, then, walked out of sight.

Astrid had stood on the pavement for a long time.

She had, at last, walked to the bus stop and had taken the number four to work.

—

She had not, in the remaining decades of her life, seen the observer again.

She had, over those decades, taken many photographs. The observer had been in none of them.

She had, from time to time, thought about that Tuesday morning. She had, from time to time, wondered whether the release had, in fact, worked — whether the observer had, at that corner on Ringvägen, been permitted, at last, to do something else. She had never, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had been given a small strange gift, known.

She had died, in her small flat in Södermalm, at seventy-eight, of the same nothing-in-particular that had taken Vera, on a small quiet morning in March.

She had, in her will, left the three albums to no one.

She had specified only that they were to be, along with the letter Vera had written her, cremated.

They had been.

The observer, so far as anyone knows, has not been seen since.

Astrid had, in the last years of her life, hoped this meant that the small careful worker had, at last, gone home. She had hoped, in her small careful way, that the release had, in the specific small formal way of a small unknown system, worked.

She had never been sure.

She had, all the same, in her last years, been quietly at peace with what she had done.

She had, in her last note to her mother — a small letter, delivered after her death — written only:

*Mother. I have loved you. I have, in my own small way, ended a small thing that had been in our family for a very long time. You did not know it. That was, all along, why it did not fall to you. I hope, on the other side of whatever is on the other side, that you understand what I mean by this.*

*Your daughter, Astrid.*

Her mother had, at eighty-three, read the letter, and had, in the small careful way of a woman who did not understand her daughters, kept it in her small drawer for the remaining years of her life, and had, at ninety-one, taken it with her.

The small drawer, when it was cleared out, had contained no photograph in whose doorway anyone unfamiliar stood.
